lead: A turbine, compressor, nozzle and boiler all keep the same account: energy carried in by the fluid plus heat added equals energy carried out plus work delivered. Because mass crosses the boundary, the energy each kilogram carries is its enthalpy plus its kinetic and potential energy, not its internal energy. Written once, with terms struck out for each device, this steady flow energy equation answers exam questions on nozzles, turbines, throttles, condensers and pumps. It is the working tool of power plants, refrigerators and air-conditioners.
prereq: You need: enthalpy, h = u + pv, and the first law with its sign convention.

sections.h3: The control volume and mass balance

blocks.text: An open system lets mass cross its boundary. We draw a fixed region in space around the device, the control volume: a turbine casing, a compressor, a radiator, a length of pipe. The fluid crosses it at the inlet 1 and the outlet 2.

blocks.where: ṁ is the mass flow rate (kg/s); ρ the density (kg/m³); A the flow area (m²); V the mean velocity (m/s); v = 1/ρ the specific volume (m³/kg).

blocks.text: The steady flow energy equation (SFEE) rests on four assumptions:

items: Steady flow: nothing inside changes with time, so mass in equals mass out, ṁ₁ = ṁ₂ = ṁ (the continuity equation, A₁V₁/v₁ = A₂V₂/v₂).
Uniform properties across each inlet and outlet section.
Constant rates of heat and work transfer.
No change in the mass or energy stored inside the control volume.

blocks.text: Per kilogram of fluid, energy in equals energy out:
h₁ + V₁²/2000 + gz₁/1000 + q = h₂ + V₂²/2000 + gz₂/1000 + w
blocks.where: h is the specific enthalpy (kJ/kg); V the velocity (m/s); z the height above a datum (m); g = 9.81 m/s²; q the heat added (kJ/kg, negative if lost); w the shaft work delivered (kJ/kg, negative if work is put in). Subscript 1 is the inlet, 2 the outlet.

blocks.text: The 2000 and 1000 are unit fixes. V²/2 comes out in J/kg, so V²/2000 is in kJ/kg; likewise gz/1000. Adding J/kg to an h in kJ/kg is the classic error.

Why enthalpy? The fluid behind the inlet pushes each kilogram in, doing flow work p₁v₁ on it, and each kilogram leaving pushes the fluid ahead, doing p₂v₂. This flow work travels with the mass, and h = u + pv already contains it, so u never appears alone.
Multiply every term by ṁ for the rate form in kW: Q̇ = ṁq is the heat transfer rate and Ẇ = ṁw the shaft power.
Every device is the same equation with some terms removed. Learn the striking out, not eight separate formulas.

head: Device
Terms dropped
Result
rows: Nozzle (speeds fluid up) or diffuser (slows it)
ΔKE, ΔPE small; q ≈ 0 if insulated
w = h₁ − h₂ (+ q if given)

blocks.text: In a throttle the pressure drops but h stays the same. An ideal gas then keeps its temperature, because its h depends on T alone. Most real gases and refrigerants cool, which is why a refrigerator has an expansion valve; hydrogen and helium at room temperature warm up instead.

A heat exchanger has two streams and no work. If it is insulated, the energy one stream loses the other gains: ṁ<sub>hot</sub>(h<sub>in</sub> − h<sub>out</sub>)<sub>hot</sub> = ṁ<sub>cold</sub>(h<sub>out</sub> − h<sub>in</sub>)<sub>cold</sub>.
Filling or emptying a tank is not steady, because the mass inside changes; that case has its own balance in Unsteady flow processes: filling and emptying of vessels.

examples.question: Steam enters a turbine at 2 kg/s with h₁ = 3200 kJ/kg, V₁ = 60 m/s and z₁ = 5 m. It leaves with h₂ = 2600 kJ/kg, V₂ = 150 m/s and z₂ = 0. The casing loses 20 kJ of heat per kg of steam. Take g = 9.81 m/s². Find the work output per kg and the power.
steps: Solve the SFEE for w: w = (h₁ − h₂) + (V₁² − V₂²)/2000 + g(z₁ − z₂)/1000 + q.
Heat is lost, so q = −20 kJ/kg.
examples.answer: w = 570.6 kJ/kg and the power is 1141.2 kW, about 1.14 MW. The kinetic term changed the answer by under 2 percent and the height term by under 0.01 percent.

examples.question: Air enters a compressor at 0.5 kg/s, 100 kPa and 300 K through a duct of area 0.04 m², and leaves at 450 K. The casing loses 10 kJ of heat per kg of air. Take R = 0.287 and c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/kg·K. Find the inlet velocity and the power input.
steps: Inlet specific volume: v₁ = RT₁/p₁ = 0.287 × 300/100 = 0.861 m³/kg.
Continuity: V₁ = ṁv₁/A₁ = 0.5 × 0.861/0.04 = 10.76 m/s. Its kinetic energy is 10.76²/2000 = 0.058 kJ/kg, negligible.
With ΔKE and ΔPE dropped: w = q + (h₁ − h₂) = q + c<sub>p</sub>(T₁ − T₂).
examples.answer: The inlet velocity is 10.8 m/s and the compressor needs 80.4 kW.

traps: Dropping ΔKE in a nozzle, where it is the answer, but keeping it in a turbine, where it is a few kJ/kg against hundreds.
Adding V²/2 in J/kg straight to h in kJ/kg. Use V²/2000 and gz/1000.
Sign of w for a compressor: w is negative and the input is h₂ − h₁ − q, not h₁ − h₂.
Using u instead of h for a flowing stream. The flow work pv crosses with the mass.
Writing h₁ = h₂ for a turbine because its casing is insulated. q = 0 does not mean h is constant; the enthalpy drop leaves as work.

quiz.q: Write the steady flow energy equation per unit mass and name every term with its unit.
quiz.a: h₁ + V₁²/2000 + gz₁/1000 + q = h₂ + V₂²/2000 + gz₂/1000 + w, with h in kJ/kg, V in m/s, z in m, g = 9.81 m/s², q the heat added and w the work delivered, both in kJ/kg.

quiz.q: Why does the SFEE use enthalpy h and not internal energy u?
quiz.a: Each kilogram crossing the boundary has flow work pv done on it at the inlet and does pv at the outlet. h = u + pv bundles that flow work with u, so h is the energy per kg that actually enters and leaves.

quiz.q: Steam flows through an insulated nozzle with h₁ = 3000 kJ/kg, V₁ = 50 m/s and h₂ = 2800 kJ/kg. Find V₂.
A refrigerant compressor takes in vapour at h₁ = 250 kJ/kg and delivers it at h₂ = 290 kJ/kg, with ṁ = 0.05 kg/s and no heat loss. Find the power input, ignoring KE and PE.
quiz.a: w = h₁ − h₂ = −40 kJ/kg, so 40 kJ/kg is put in. Power = 0.05 × 40 = 2 kW.

quiz.q: Why can a pump’s work input be written as v(p₂ − p₁)?
quiz.a: A liquid is nearly incompressible and barely warms in a pump, so u₂ ≈ u₁ and h₂ − h₁ = (u₂ − u₁) + v(p₂ − p₁) ≈ v(p₂ − p₁).

quiz.q: A throttle keeps h constant. Why does an ideal gas keep its temperature while most real gases cool?
quiz.a: For an ideal gas h depends on T alone, so h₁ = h₂ forces T₁ = T₂. A real gas has h depending on both T and p, so a pressure drop at constant h shifts T: most gases cool at room temperature (the Joule-Thomson effect), hydrogen and helium warm.

quiz.q: In a turbine we may ignore the kinetic-energy term but in a nozzle we cannot. Justify both.
quiz.a: In the turbine example ΔKE is −9.45 kJ/kg against a 600 kJ/kg enthalpy drop, under 2 percent. A nozzle exists to turn enthalpy into velocity, so its kinetic-energy gain equals the whole enthalpy drop; dropping it removes the answer.

beyond: Steam-plant designers combine the SFEE with turbine and pump maps, and refrigeration engineers use the isenthalpic throttle as the standard expansion step. Exergy analysis then rates each term by how much of it could become work. Computational fluid dynamics drops the uniform-section assumption and lets h, V and z vary across a section. Search: control volume energy balance, flow work, nozzle efficiency, Joule-Thomson coefficient.
